clue.text: Throw in a diamond

parts.note: a baseball field is called a diamond, and the delivery a hurler sends to the batter there has its own name

explanation.definitionFit: In baseball, played on a diamond, each delivery the hurler sends to the batter has this name.

clue.text: Publication where you'll find daily puzzle

definitions.text: Publication where you'll find daily puzzle

parts.words: Publication where you'll find daily puzzle
parts.note: reads like a puzzle book, but split it into the daily newspaper's rear page, where crosswords traditionally sit

explanation.definitionFit: A soft-covered book is one kind of publication, and the rear page of a daily newspaper is where the crossword sits.

clue.text: He turns up set of clothes, including type of shirt

indicators.note: including means one piece holds another inside
turns up, in a down clue, means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a suit is a matching set of clothes
a T-shirt is a type of shirt

explanation.surface: A man arrives wearing a suit and a particular kind of shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns up' reverses SUIT to TIUS, and 'including' puts T inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman emperor and the Shakespeare tragedy's title figure both bear this male name.

clue.text: Having loaf on fire is so rash

parts.note: on fire means burning hot
loaf is slang for head, so having one is being headed

explanation.surface: Setting fire to a loaf of bread is a reckless act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaf' is the bread but also slang for the head, as in 'use your loaf'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hothead acts impulsively, so the adjective means impetuous.

clue.text: It provides blanket coverage — for dorm feast?

parts.note: a dorm is full of beds, and here the word stands for the place one sleeps
a spread is a lavish meal laid out on a table

explanation.surface: A midnight feast in a school dormitory is described as covering everything like a blanket.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads the answer as a feast eaten in bed, the classic boarding-school midnight treat.
explanation.definitionFit: A cover laid over the blankets of a made bed, so it literally gives blanket coverage.

clue.text: Rose, perhaps, or Amelia

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the woman is Rose or Amelia.
explanation.walkthrough: Amelia Bloomer was the 19th-century American campaigner after whom bloomers (loose trousers for women) were named.
explanation.definitionFit: A flowering plant is one that blossoms, and the reformer Amelia Bloomer gave her surname to women's trousers.

clue.text: Get order confused and explode grenade

indicators.note: exploding blows something apart, so the letters fly into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Muddled orders end with a grenade going off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'explode' rearranges the letters of GRENADE.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw into disorder is to disarrange, the older sense of the word.

clue.text: Field for fair person (according to Johnson)

explanation.surface: A meadow suits a fair-minded person, if you believe Dr Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr Johnson quipped that the Irish are a fair people, for they never speak well of one another; Paddy is a nickname for an Irishman.
explanation.definitionFit: A rice field is a paddy, and an Irishman by nickname is one too, the people Johnson called 'fair'.

clue.text: Surrender to another country

parts.note: surrender looks like giving up in war, but here it is handing a suspect over to a foreign state's courts

explanation.definitionFit: Legally handing over an accused person to the state where the crime was committed.

clue.text: French writer in Russian councils

explanation.surface: A French novelist sits in on Russian assemblies.
explanation.walkthrough: The Duma is the Russian parliament; Alexandre Dumas wrote The Three Musketeers.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandre Dumas wrote The Three Musketeers, and a duma is a Russian elected assembly.

clue.text: Poet involved with fruit cake

indicators.note: involved here means tangled up together, so the letters of the two words are mixed

explanation.surface: A poet gets mixed up in a fruit cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' mixes the letters of POET and FRUIT together.
explanation.definitionFit: A petit four is a small fancy iced cake served with coffee.

clue.text: Trade union in current stoppage, in fact

indicators.note: in tells us one piece sits inside the other in this clue

parts.note: a dam stops the current of a river

explanation.surface: A union strike halts work, in fact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'current stoppage' sounds like an industrial dispute, but it is a barrier stopping a river's current.
explanation.definitionFit: A datum is a single piece of information or given quantity, singular of data.

clue.text: Cider-drinker or wine type I included

indicators.note: included signals that one piece is taken inside another

parts.note: rosé is a pink type of wine

explanation.surface: Someone drinking cider, or a type of wine with I added.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cider with Rosie' is Laurie Lee's memoir of a Cotswold boyhood, in which Rosie shares cider with the narrator.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurie Lee's memoir Cider with Rosie has the girl who shares the drink with the young narrator.

clue.text: Dives for coins a great deal

parts.note: coins are cash, that is money
bags of something means a large amount of it

explanation.surface: A diver plunges for coins worth a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Dives is the rich man in the Bible parable of Dives and Lazarus, not a verb about diving.
explanation.definitionFit: Dives is the traditional name for the rich man of the parable, so a wealthy person.

clue.text: Apart from Roman coin below

parts.note: the as was a bronze coin of ancient Rome
below means under

explanation.surface: Something set apart from a Roman coin lying underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Torn apart and in pieces are both meanings of the word, as in 'let no man put asunder'.

clue.text: Forced flat, perhaps?

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a strained performance is a little flat.
explanation.walkthrough: In music a natural is a note neither sharp nor flat, so a flat is not natural.
explanation.definitionFit: Forced means strained and artificial; a musical flat, being no natural, is literally not natural.

clue.text: Is this disease a type of shingles, almost?

indicators.note: a type of suggests a variant form, so the letters are rearranged
almost means the last letter of the word is dropped

explanation.surface: A doctor asks whether an illness is a variety of shingles, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the last S of shingles to leave SHINGLE; 'a type of' rearranges that. 'The English disease' is a nickname once used for rickets and later for strikes.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'the English disease' was a nickname for rickets and later for industrial unrest, so the word names this illness.

clue.text: Ridley's train won't pull out — the place is deserted

parts.note: Arnold Ridley wrote the stage thriller The Ghost Train, so his train is a ghost one

indicators.note: pull out here means wrench into a different shape, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Ridley's locomotive refuses to leave the station, because the place is empty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pull out' rearranges WONT into TOWN. 'Ridley's train' is from The Ghost Train, Arnold Ridley's 1920s play.
explanation.definitionFit: An abandoned settlement with no inhabitants left is described this way.

clue.text: Commiseration for players' difficulty

explanation.surface: Sympathy is offered to actors struggling with their roles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard lines!' is a British way to say 'bad luck'; players here are actors with tricky lines to learn.
explanation.definitionFit: A British exclamation of sympathy for bad luck, and also tricky speeches an actor must learn.

clue.text: Making do? Maybe that conceals our state

indicators.note: conceals says the letters lie inside the clue's words

explanation.surface: Someone getting by with little wonders whether that hides the country's condition.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'maKING DO Maybe'.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain is the United Kingdom, so for a British setter the realm is our state.

clue.text: Like ill-disposed characters

parts.note: ill-disposed suggests hostile people, but read it as roles badly allotted to actors

explanation.definitionFit: Roles given to unsuitable actors are badly allocated, just as characters ill-disposed in a play are.

clue.text: 23's blazer has one in support

indicators.note: in shows one piece is set inside the other here

parts.note: a pier is a supporting pillar of a bridge or arch
taken as written

explanation.surface: A blazer jacket worn by someone has one more for support.
explanation.walkthrough: 23 is TRAIL, so '23's blazer' is a trailblazer.
explanation.definitionFit: A trailblazer is a person who leads the way into new ground.

clue.text: Crossing the channel

parts.note: suggests a ferry to France, but also a corridor or the journey by sea itself

explanation.definitionFit: A sea voyage, such as a ferry trip, is so called, as is a corridor from one place to another.

clue.text: Opening lots of letters, they may share our secrets

parts.note: a gate is an opening in a fence or wall
post means mail, so posts are deliveries of letters

explanation.surface: Someone opening a pile of letters fears they will share our secrets.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'between you and me and the gatepost' marks something told in confidence.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'between you, me and the gatepost' makes these fence uprights the keepers of confidences.

clue.text: Such an informer may be bent

definitions.text: Such an informer may be bent

parts.words: Such an informer may be bent
parts.note: bent suggests a corrupt police informer, but bent is also a kind of lawn plant

explanation.definitionFit: British slang calls a police informer this, and bent is one species of the lawn plant.

clue.text: Snap — or nip?

parts.note: in a down clue the word pin written upwards spells nip

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to take a quick photo or a little pinch.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer as instructions, PIN written UP in a down grid, gives 'nip'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pin-up is a photograph of an attractive person, and a snap is an informal photo.

clue.text: Drag behind rear section? That's about right

indicators.note: about here means going round, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: the tail is the rear section of an animal or aircraft

explanation.surface: Something drags behind at the back; that seems about right.
explanation.definitionFit: To trail is to be pulled along behind, as a cloak trails on the ground.

clue.text: Reproducing a bullet's sound

parts.note: a ping is the sharp ringing noise of a bullet striking metal

explanation.surface: A recording copies the noise a bullet makes.
explanation.definitionFit: Mimicking is copying like an ape, so it means imitating or reproducing.

clue.text: Stage part Adam created for himself

explanation.surface: An actor playing Adam in a stage show makes his own part.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis Adam and Eve sewed fig leaves into coverings, called aprons in the King James Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: The forestage in front of the curtain has this name; Genesis says Adam and Eve sewed fig leaves into such coverings.

clue.text: A national disaster for a Turk

indicators.note: a disaster wrecks things, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A national catastrophe befalls a person from Turkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disaster' scrambles the letters of A NATIONAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatolia is the Asian heartland of Turkey, so someone from there is Turkish.

clue.text: Preservative makes Jack safe, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the letters follow how the words are spoken

parts.note: jack and salt are both slang for a sailor; peter is old criminal slang for a safe

explanation.surface: A safe-cracker named Jack is said to make a preserving agent.
explanation.walkthrough: SALT (sailor, like Jack) and PETER (thieves' slang for a safe) together sound like the chemical.
explanation.definitionFit: Potassium nitrate has long been used to cure meats such as bacon and ham.

clue.text: This emperor sometimes got drunk

explanation.surface: An emperor who now and then hit the bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of the Ethiopian ruler, and also a hot drink of port or sherry with sugar and spice.
